claim: Myxococcus xanthus is a Gram-negative bacterium that glides on solid surfaces.
source: The Gram-negative bacterium Myxococcus xanthus glides on solid surfaces.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract of the manuscript.

claim: Dynamic bacterial focal adhesion complexes (bFACs) convert proton motive force from the inner membrane into mechanical propulsion on the cell surface.
source: Dynamic bacterial focal adhesion complexes (bFACs) convert proton motive force from the inner membrane into mechanical propulsion on the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: AgmT is a highly abundant lytic PG transglycosylase homologous to Escherichia coli MltG.
source: Here, we show that AgmT, a highly abundant lytic PG transglycosylase homologous to Escherichia coli MltG, couples bFACs to PG.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by sequence analysis and experimental data showing LTG activity.

claim: AgmT couples bFACs to peptidoglycan (PG).
source: Here, we show that AgmT, a highly abundant lytic PG transglycosylase homologous to Escherichia coli MltG, couples bFACs to PG.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by coprecipitation assays and single-particle microscopy.

claim: Gliding motors fail to connect to PG in the absence of an active AgmT.
source: Coprecipitation assay and single-particle microscopy reveal that the gliding motors fail to connect to PG and thus are unable to assemble into bFACs in the absence of an active AgmT.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from coprecipitation assays and single-particle tracking.

claim: Gliding motors are unable to assemble into bFACs in the absence of an active AgmT.
source: Coprecipitation assay and single-particle microscopy reveal that the gliding motors fail to connect to PG and thus are unable to assemble into bFACs in the absence of an active AgmT.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by single-particle tracking data showing reduced stationary populations of AglR.

claim: Heterologous expression of E. coli MltG restores the connection between PG and bFACs in M. xanthus cells that lack AgmT.
source: Heterologous expression of E. coli MltG restores the connection between PG and bFACs and thus rescues gliding motility in the M. xanthus cells that lack AgmT.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by gliding motility assays and coprecipitation experiments.

claim: Heterologous expression of E. coli MltG rescues gliding motility in M. xanthus cells that lack AgmT.
source: Heterologous expression of E. coli MltG restores the connection between PG and bFACs and thus rescues gliding motility in the M. xanthus cells that lack AgmT.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by colony edge assays and single-cell tracking data.

claim: bFACs anchor to AgmT-modified PG to transmit mechanical force across the PG cell wall.
source: Our results indicate that bFACs anchor to AgmT-modified PG to transmit mechanical force across the PG cell wall.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the collective experimental evidence.

claim: Surface-associated motility is critical for many bacteria to navigate and populate their environments.
source: Surface-associated motility is critical for many bacteria to navigate and populate their environments (Nan and Zusman, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: M. xanthus moves on solid surfaces using two independent mechanisms: social (S-) motility and adventurous (A-) motility.
source: The Gram-negative bacterium Myxococcus xanthus moves on solid surfaces using two independent mechanisms: social (S-) motility and adventurous (A-) motility.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge about M. xanthus.

claim: S-motility is analogous to twitching motility in Pseudomonas and Neisseria and is powered by the extension and retraction of type IV pili.
source: S-motility, analogous to the twitching motility in Pseudomonas and Neisseria, is powered by the extension and retraction of type IV pili (Chang et al., 2016; Wu and Kaiser, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: A-motility is a form of gliding motility that does not depend on conventional motility-related cell surface appendages, such as flagella or pili.
source: A-motility is a form of gliding motility that does not depend on conventional motility-related cell surface appendages, such as flagella or pili (Nan and Zusman, 2016; Nan and Zusman, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: AglR, AglQ, and AglS form a membrane channel that functions as the gliding motor by harvesting proton motive force.
source: AglR, AglQ, and AglS form a membrane channel that functions as the gliding motor by harvesting proton motive force (Nan et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Motor units associate with at least 14 gliding-related proteins that reside in the cytoplasm, inner membrane, periplasm, and outer membrane.
source: Motor units associate with at least 14 gliding-related proteins that reside in the cytoplasm, inner membrane, periplasm, and outer membrane (Jakobczak et al., 2015; Nan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: In each gliding cell, two distinct populations of gliding complexes coexist: dynamic complexes move along helical paths and static complexes remain fixed relative to the substrate.
source: In each gliding cell, two distinct populations of gliding complexes coexist: dynamic complexes move along helical paths and static complexes remain fixed relative to the substrate (Faure et al., 2016; Nan et al., 2013; Nan et al., 2014; Nan, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Motors transport incomplete gliding complexes along helical tracks but form complete, force-generating complexes at the ventral side of cells that appear fixed to the substrate.
source: Motors transport incomplete gliding complexes along helical tracks but form complete, force-generating complexes at the ventral side of cells that appear fixed to the substrate (Figure 1; Faure et al., 2016; Nan, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations and Figure 1.

claim: Complete gliding machineries are called bacterial focal adhesion complexes (bFACs) based on their functional analogy with eukaryotic focal adhesion sites.
source: Based on their functional analogy with eukaryotic focal adhesion sites, these complete gliding machineries are called bacterial focal adhesion complexes (bFACs).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: Individual motors frequently display move–stall–move patterns, in which they move rapidly along helical trajectories, join a bFAC where they remain stationary briefly, then move rapidly again toward the next bFAC or reverse their moving directions.
source: Individual motors frequently display move–stall–move patterns, in which they move rapidly along helical trajectories, join a bFAC where they remain stationary briefly, then move rapidly again toward the next bFAC or reverse their moving directions (Nan et al., 2013; Nan et al., 2015; Pogue et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: bFACs adhere to the gliding substrate through an outer membrane adhesin.
source: bFACs adhere to the gliding substrate through an outer membrane adhesin (Islam et al., 2023; Nan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: As motors transport bFACs toward lagging cell poles, cells move forward but bFACs remain static relative to the gliding substrate.
source: As motors transport bFACs toward lagging cell poles, cells move forward but bFACs remain static relative to the gliding substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: bFAC assembly can be quantified at nanometer resolution using the single-particle dynamics of gliding motors.
source: bFAC assembly can be quantified at nanometer resolution using the single-particle dynamics of gliding motors (Nan et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Single particles of a fully functional, photoactivatable mCherry (PAmCherry)-labeled AglR display three dynamic patterns: stationary, directed motion, and diffusion.
source: Single particles of a fully functional, photoactivatable mCherry (PAmCherry)-labeled AglR display three dynamic patterns, stationary, directed motion, and diffusion (Nan et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The stationary population consists of the motors in fully assembled bFACs, which do not move before photobleach.
source: The stationary population consists of the motors in fully assembled bFACs, which do not move before photobleach.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on previous work.

claim: Motors moving in a directed manner carry incomplete gliding complexes along helical tracks.
source: In contrast, the motors moving in a directed manner carry incomplete gliding complexes along helical tracks, whereas the diffusing motors assemble to even less completeness (Faure et al., 2016; Nan et al., 2013; Nan, 2017; Fu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Diffusing motors assemble to even less completeness than motors moving in a directed manner.
source: In contrast, the motors moving in a directed manner carry incomplete gliding complexes along helical tracks, whereas the diffusing motors assemble to even less completeness (Faure et al., 2016; Nan et al., 2013; Nan, 2017; Fu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Motors only generate force in static bFACs.
source: As motors only generate force in static bFACs (Faure et al., 2016), the population of nonmotile motors indicates the overall status of fully assembled bFACs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The population of nonmotile motors indicates the overall status of fully assembled bFACs.
source: As motors only generate force in static bFACs (Faure et al., 2016), the population of nonmotile motors indicates the overall status of fully assembled bFACs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on inference from previous work.

claim: PG is a mesh-like single molecule of crosslinked glycan strands that surrounds the entire cytoplasmic membrane.
source: PG is a mesh-like single molecule of crosslinked glycan strands that surrounds the entire cytoplasmic membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge about peptidoglycan.

claim: The rigidity of PG defines cell shape and protects cells from osmotic lysis.
source: The rigidity of PG defines cell shape and protects cells from osmotic lysis (Garner, 2021; Rohs and Bernhardt, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: If bFACs physically penetrate PG, their transportation toward lagging cell poles would tear PG and trigger cell lysis.
source: If bFACs physically penetrate PG, their transportation toward lagging cell poles would tear PG and trigger cell lysis.
evidence: This is a logical inference stated in the introduction.

claim: Rather than forming stable and rigid complexes, gliding-related proteins only assemble into force-generating machineries in bFACs.
source: To avoid breaching PG, an updated model proposes that rather than forming stable and rigid complexes, gliding-related proteins only assemble into force-generating machineries in bFACs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Outside of bFACs, gliding-related proteins could localize diffusively or move along with unengaged motor units.
source: Outside of bFACs, these proteins could localize diffusively or move along with unengaged motor units (Faure et al., 2016; Chen and Nan, 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The inner subcomplexes, containing the motors, are the force-generating units in bFACs.
source: The inner subcomplexes, containing the motors, are the force-generating units in bFACs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on the model of bFAC function.

claim: To transmit force to the cell surface, the inner subcomplexes must push against two relatively rigid structures, one on each side of the membrane, in opposite directions.
source: As motors reside in the fluid inner membrane, to transmit force to the cell surface, the inner subcomplexes must push against two relatively rigid structures, one on each side of the membrane, in opposite directions (Chen and Nan, 2022; Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation and Figure 1.

claim: MreB is a bacterial actin homolog that supports rod shape in many bacteria.
source: MreB is a bacterial actin homolog that supports rod shape in many bacteria (Fu et al., 2018; Garner, 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: In M. xanthus, MreB connects to bFACs on the cytoplasmic side and plays essential roles in gliding.
source: In M. xanthus, MreB also connects to bFACs on the cytoplasmic side and thus plays essential roles in gliding (Nan and Zusman, 2016; Nan and Zusman, 2011; Nan et al., 2011; Nan et al., 2014; Fu et al., 2018; Mauriello et al., 2010; Treuner-Lange et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The inner subcomplexes could push against MreB filaments and PG in the cytoplasm and periplasm, respectively.
source: The inner subcomplexes could push against MreB filaments and PG in the cytoplasm and periplasm, respectively (Faure et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2018; Chen and Nan, 2022; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The interaction between the inner subcomplexes and PG not only satisfies the physical requirement for force generation but also supports bFAC stability.
source: The interaction between the inner subcomplexes and PG not only satisfies the physical requirement for force generation but also supports bFAC stability.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on inference.

claim: Without the interaction between inner subcomplexes and PG, the inner and outer subcomplexes can only form transient, 'slippery' association, which is predicted to produce short and aberrant cell movements.
source: Without this interaction, the inner and outer subcomplexes can only form transient, 'slippery' association, which is predicted to produce short and aberrant cell movements (Chen and Nan, 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: It was speculated that gliding motors in the inner complex could bind PG directly.
source: It was speculated that gliding motors in the inner complex could bind PG directly (Faure et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Direct binding of gliding motors to PG has not been confirmed by experiments.
source: However, such binding has not been confirmed by experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: AgmT is required for M. xanthus gliding motility.
source: In this study, we found that AgmT, a lytic transglycosylase (LTG) for PG, is required for M. xanthus gliding motility.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: AgmT only regulates cell morphology moderately during vegetative growth.
source: Whereas AgmT only regulates cell morphology moderately during vegetative growth, it is essential for maintaining PG integrity under the stress from the antibiotic mecillinam.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: AgmT is essential for maintaining PG integrity under the stress from the antibiotic mecillinam.
source: Whereas AgmT only regulates cell morphology moderately during vegetative growth, it is essential for maintaining PG integrity under the stress from the antibiotic mecillinam.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: AgmT is essential for the inner subcomplexes to connect to PG and stall in bFACs.
source: Using single-particle tracking microscopy and coprecipitation assays, we found that AgmT is essential for the inner subcomplexes to connect to PG and stall in bFACs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: Expressing E. coli MltG heterologously rescues the connection between PG and bFACs.
source: Importantly, expressing Escherichia coli MltG heterologously rescues the connection between PG and bFACs and thus restores gliding motility.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: The LTG activity of AgmT anchors bFACs to PG, potentially by modifying PG structure.
source: Hence, the LTG activity of AgmT anchors bFACs to PG, potentially by modifying PG structure.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: AgmT showed significant similarity to the widely conserved YceG/MltG family LTGs.
source: After careful analysis, we found that AgmT showed significant similarity to the widely conserved YceG/MltG family LTGs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence analysis.

claim: The putative active site of AgmT, Glu223, is conserved.
source: The putative active site, Glu223 (corresponding to E218 in E. coli MltG) (Yunck et al., 2016), is conserved in AgmT (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ΔagmT pilA− cells formed sharp colony edges on agar surface, indicating that they could not move efficiently with gliding.
source: Similarly, the ΔagmT pilA− cells also formed sharp colony edges, indicating that they could not move efficiently with gliding (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Individual ΔagmT pilA− cells displayed slow movements, with frequent pauses and reversals.
source: To our surprise, instead of being static, individual ΔagmT pilA− cells displayed slow movements, with frequent pauses and reversals (Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Video 1.

claim: ΔagmT pilA− cells moved significantly slower (0.88 ± 0.62 μm/min, n = 59) compared to pilA− cells (2.30 ± 1.33 μm/min, n = 46).
source: Compared to the pilA− cells that moved at 2.30 ± 1.33 μm/min (n = 46) and high persistency (Video 2 and Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 2), ΔagmT pilA− cells moved significantly slower (0.88 ± 0.62 μm/min, n = 59) and less persistent (Video 1 and Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ΔagmT pilA− cells moved less persistently than pilA− cells.
source: Compared to the pilA− cells that moved at 2.30 ± 1.33 μm/min (n = 46) and high persistency (Video 2 and Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 2), ΔagmT pilA− cells moved significantly slower (0.88 ± 0.62 μm/min, n = 59) and less persistent (Video 1 and Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The slow and 'slippery' gliding of the ΔagmT pilA− cells matches the prediction that when the inner complexes of bFACs lose connection with PG, bFACs can only generate short, and inefficient movements.
source: Instead, the slow and 'slippery' gliding of the ΔagmT pilA− cells matches the prediction that when the inner complexes of bFACs lose connection with PG, bFACs can only generate short, and inefficient movements (Chen and Nan, 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: AgmT is not an essential component in the bFACs.
source: Our data indicate that AgmT is not an essential component in the bFACs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the observation that cells lacking AgmT still show some motility.

claim: AgmT is likely to regulate the assembly and stability of bFACs, especially their connection with PG.
source: Thus, AgmT is likely to regulate the assembly and stability of bFACs, especially their connection with PG.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on inference from the data.

claim: The putative LTG activity of AgmT is required for gliding.
source: As AgmT is a putative LTG for PG, we then tested if its predicted active site, Glu223, is required for gliding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data showing that agmTEAEA pilA− cells formed sharp colony edges.

claim: agmTEAEA pilA− cells formed sharp colony edges on agar surface.
source: Because the amino acid following Glu223 is also a glutamate (Glu224), we replaced both glutamate residues with alanine (AgmTEAEA) using site-directed mutagenesis to alter their codons on the chromosome. agmTEAEA pilA− cells formed sharp colony edges on agar surface (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Wild-type AgmT solubilized dye-labeled M. xanthus PG that absorbed light at 595 nm.
source: Similar to lysozyme that specifically cleaves the β-1,4-glycosidic bonds in PG, wild-type AgmT solubilized dye-labeled M. xanthus PG that absorbed light at 595 nm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The AgmTEAEA variant failed to release the dye from labeled PG.
source: In contrast, the AgmTEAEA variant failed to release the dye (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AgmT displays LTG activity in vitro.
source: Hence, AgmT displays LTG activity in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the RBB assay data.

claim: Cells that lack AgmT and express AgmTEAEA are significantly shorter and wider than wild-type cells.
source: Whereas AgmT does not affect growth rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), cells that lacked AgmT or expressed AgmTEAEA maintained rod shape but were slightly shorter and wider than the wild-type ones (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Altered morphology alone does not likely account for abolished gliding.
source: Nevertheless, altered morphology alone does not likely account for abolished gliding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparison with the Δ3 mutant.

claim: A mutant that lacks all three class A penicillin-binding proteins (Δ3) displays similarly shortened and widened morphology but is still motile by gliding.
source: In fact, a previously reported mutant that lacks all three class A penicillin-binding proteins (Δ3) displays similarly shortened and widened morphology (Zhang et al., 2023) but is still motile by gliding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: V. cholerae MltG degrades un-crosslinked PG turnover products and prevents their detrimental accumulation in the periplasm.
source: A recent report revealed that Vibrio cholerae MltG degrades un-crosslinked PG turnover products and prevents their detrimental accumulation in the periplasm (Weaver et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Mecillinam is a β-lactam that induces the production of toxic, un-crosslinked PG strands.
source: Mecillinam is a β-lactam that induces the production of toxic, un-crosslinked PG strands (Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Wild-type M. xanthus can largely mitigate mecillinam stress.
source: Rather than collapsing the rod shape, mecillinam only causes bulging near the centers of wild-type M. xanthus cells, whereas large-scale cell lysis does not occur, and cell poles still maintain rod shape even after prolonged (20 hr) treatment (Figure 3C; Zhang et al., 2023). Thus, wild-type M. xanthus can largely mitigate mecillinam stress.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mecillinam-treated agmT cells increased their width drastically, displayed significant cell surface irregularity along their entire cell bodies, and lysed frequently.
source: In contrast, mecillinam-treated agmT cells increased their width drastically, displayed significant cell surface irregularity along their entire cell bodies, and lysed frequently (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cells expressing AgmTEAEA as the sole source of AgmT displayed similar, but even stronger phenotypes under mecillinam stress, growing into elongated, twisted filaments that formed multiple cell poles and lysed frequently.
source: Cells expressing AgmTEAEA as the sole source of AgmT displayed similar, but even stronger phenotypes under mecillinam stress, growing into elongated, twisted filaments that formed multiple cell poles and lysed frequently (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Similar to V. cholerae MltG, M. xanthus AgmT is important for maintaining cell integrity under mecillinam stress.
source: These results confirm that similar to V. cholerae MltG, M. xanthus AgmT is important for maintaining cell integrity under mecillinam stress.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the mecillinam stress data.

claim: While other LTGs could partially substitute AgmT, AgmTEAEA blocks these enzymes from accessing un-crosslinked PG strands.
source: The different responses from agmT and agmTEAEA cells suggest that while other LTGs could partially substitute AgmT, AgmTEAEA blocks these enzymes from accessing un-crosslinked PG strands.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on inference from the data.

claim: AgmT is the only LTG in M. xanthus that belongs to the YceG/MltG family.
source: AgmT is the only LTG in M. xanthus that belongs to the YceG/MltG family.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The genome of M. xanthus contains 13 genes that encode putative LTGs besides agmT.
source: Besides agmT, the genome of M. xanthus contains 13 genes that encode putative LTGs (Key resources table).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the Key resources table.

claim: Mutants lacking each of the 13 other putative LTG genes all retained gliding motility.
source: To test if these proteins also contribute to gliding, we knocked out each of these 13 genes in the pilA− background. The resulting mutants all retained gliding motility, indicating that AgmT is the only LTG that is required for M. xanthus gliding (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: AgmT is the only LTG that is required for M. xanthus gliding.
source: To test if these proteins also contribute to gliding, we knocked out each of these 13 genes in the pilA− background. The resulting mutants all retained gliding motility, indicating that AgmT is the only LTG that is required for M. xanthus gliding (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data.

claim: 32.1% (n = 2700) of AglR-PAmCherry particles remained within one pixel (160 nm × 160 nm) before photobleach, indicating that they were immotile.
source: Consistent with our previous results (Nan et al., 2013; Nan et al., 2015), 32.1% (n = 2700) of AglR-PAmCherry particles remained within one pixel (160 nm × 160 nm) before photobleach, indicating that they were immotile.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sptPALM data.

claim: The remaining 67.9% AglR-PAmCherry particles were motile, leaving trajectories of various lengths.
source: The remaining 67.9% AglR-PAmCherry particles were motile, leaving trajectories of various lengths (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: bFAC assembly is sensitive to mechanical cues.
source: bFAC assembly is sensitive to mechanical cues.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data showing changes in bFAC assembly with agar concentration.

claim: As the agar concentration increases in gliding substrate, more motor molecules engage in bFACs, where they appear immotile.
source: As the agar concentration increases in gliding substrate, more motor molecules engage in bFACs, where they appear immotile (Nan et al., 2010; Nan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: As the agar concentration increased, bFACs increased significantly in size.
source: As the agar concentration increased, bFACs increased significantly in size (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The immotile AglR particles detected by sptPALM increased from 10.7% (n = 1112) on 0.5% agar to 45.2% (n = 726) on 5.0% agar surface.
source: Accordingly, the immotile AglR particles detected by sptPALM increased from 10.7% (n = 1112) on 0.5% agar to 45.2% (n = 726) on 5.0% agar surface (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The stationary population of AglR-PAmCherry particles reflects the AglR molecules in fully assembled bFACs.
source: Thus, the stationary population of AglR-PAmCherry particles reflects the AglR molecules in fully assembled bFACs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on inference from the data.

claim: AglR particles were hyper motile in the cells that lacked AgmT or expressed AgmTEAEA.
source: In contrast to the cells that expressed wild-type AgmT (agmT+), AglR particles were hyper motile in the cells that lacked AgmT or expressed AgmTEAEA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sptPALM data.

claim: On 1.5% agar surfaces, the immotile populations of AglR particles decreased to 10.5% (n = 2989) in ΔagmT cells and 11.7% (n = 1408) in agmTEAEA cells.
source: On 1.5% agar surfaces, the immotile populations of AglR particles decreased to 10.5% (n = 2989) and 11.7% (n = 1408), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AglR-containing bFACs were rarely detectable in cells lacking AgmT or expressing AgmTEAEA, even on 5% agar surfaces.
source: Consistently, AglR-containing bFACs were rarely detectable in these cells, even on 5% agar surfaces (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: In the cells that expressed wild-type AgmT, YFP-labeled AglZ formed a bright cluster at the leading cell pole and multiple static, near-evenly spaced clusters along the cell body, indicating the assembly of bFACs.
source: In the cells that expressed wild-type AgmT, yellow fluorescent protein (YFP)-labeled AglZ formed a bright cluster at the leading cell pole and multiple static, near-evenly spaced clusters along the cell body, indicating the assembly of bFACs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: AglZ-YFP only formed single clusters at cell poles in the cells that lacked AgmT or expressed AgmTEAEA.
source: In contrast, AglZ-YFP only formed single clusters at cell poles in the cells that lacked AgmT or expressed AgmTEAEA (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The LTG activity of AgmT is essential for proper bFACs assembly.
source: Taken together, the LTG activity of AgmT is essential for proper bFACs assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is the conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: agmT-PAmCherry pilA- cells displayed gliding motility that was indistinguishable from pilA− cells, indicating that the fusion protein is functional.
source: agmT-PAmCherry pilA- cells displayed gliding motility that was indistinguishable from pilA− cells (Figure 2B), indicating that the fusion protein is functional.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AgmT-PAmCherry accumulated in two bands in SDS–PAGE that corresponded to monomers and dimers of the full-length fusion protein.
source: Similar to many membrane proteins that are resistant to dissociation by sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) (Rath et al., 2009), immunoblot using an anti-mCherry antibody showed that AgmT-PAmCherry accumulated in two bands in SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) that corresponded to monomers and dimers of the full-length fusion protein, respectively (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: This result is consistent with the structure of E. coli MltG that functions as homodimers.
source: This result is consistent with the structure of E. coli MltG that functions as homodimers (PDB: 2r1f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: AgmT-PAmCherry was about 50 times more abundant than AglR-PAmCherry.
source: Importantly, AgmT-PAmCherry was about 50 times more abundant than AglR-PAmCherry (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: On a 1.5% agar surface that favors gliding motility, AglZ formed bright clusters at cell poles and aggregated in near-evenly spaced bFACs along the cell body, while AgmT localized near evenly along cell bodies without forming protein clusters.
source: We found that on a 1.5% agar surface that favors gliding motility, AglZ formed bright clusters at cell poles and aggregated in near-evenly spaced bFACs along the cell body. In contrast, AgmT localized near evenly along cell bodies without forming protein clusters (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: AgmT does not localize into bFACs.
source: Thus, AgmT does not localize into bFACs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the localization data.

claim: Despite its abundance, AgmT has not been identified as a component in bFACs despite extensive pull-down experiments using various bFAC components as baits.
source: These results echo the fact that despite its abundance, AgmT has not been identified as a component in bFACs despite extensive pull-down experiments using various bFAC components as baits (Nan et al., 2011; Nan et al., 2010; Jolivet et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: AgmT moved in a diffusive manner, showing no significant immotile population.
source: Distinct from the AglR particles of which 32.1% remained stationary, AgmT moved in a diffusive manner, showing no significant immotile population.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sptPALM data.

claim: AgmT particles diffused much faster (D = 2.9 × 10−2 ± 5.3 × 10−3 μm2/s (n = 8548)) compared to the diffusion coefficients of motile AglR particles (1.8 × 10−2 ± 3.6 × 10−3 μm2/s (n = 1833)).
source: Importantly, compared to the diffusion coefficients (D) of motile AglR particles (1.8 × 10−2 ± 3.6 × 10−3 μm2/s (n = 1833)), AgmT particles diffused much faster (D = 2.9 × 10−2 ± 5.3 × 10−3 μm2/s (n = 8548)).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sptPALM data.

claim: AgmT and the gliding motor did not display significant correlation in either their localization or dynamics.
source: Taken together, AgmT and the gliding motor did not display significant correlation in either their localization or dynamics.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the localization and dynamics data.

claim: AgmT does not assemble into bFACs.
source: We thus conclude that AgmT does not assemble into bFACs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is the conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Induced by 200 μM sodium vanillate, MltGEc restored cell morphology and integrity of the ΔagmT strain to the wild-type level.
source: Induced by 200 μM sodium vanillate, MltGEc restored cell morphology and integrity of the ΔagmT strain to the wild-type level (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: This result confirmed that MltGEc was expressed and enzymatically active in M. xanthus.
source: This result confirmed that MltGEc was expressed and enzymatically active in M. xanthus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the mecillinam resistance data.

claim: MltGEc failed to confer mecillinam resistance to the agmTEAEA cells.
source: In contrast, MltGEc failed to confer mecillinam resistance to the agmTEAEA cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: AgmTEAEA could still bind to PG and thus block MltGEc from accessing M. xanthus PG.
source: A potential explanation is that AgmTEAEA could still bind to PG and thus block MltGEc from accessing M. xanthus PG.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a speculation based on the data.

claim: The expression of MltGEc restored gliding motility of the ΔagmT pilA− cells on both the colony and single-cell levels.
source: Consistent with its LTG activity, the expression of MltGEc restored gliding motility of the ΔagmT pilA− cells on both the colony (Figure 2B) and single-cell (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 2) levels.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 2B, 2C, and 2D.

claim: In the absence of sodium vanillate, the leakage expression of MltGEc using the vanillate-inducible promoter was sufficient to compensate the loss of AgmT.
source: Interestingly, in the absence of sodium vanillate, the leakage expression of MltGEc using the vanillate-inducible promoter was sufficient to compensate the loss of AgmT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the gliding motility data.

claim: As E. coli grows much faster (generation time 20–30 min) than M. xanthus (generation time ~4 hr), MltGEc could possess significantly higher LTG activity than AgmT.
source: A plausible explanation of this observation is that as E. coli grows much faster (generation time 20–30 min) than M. xanthus (generation time ~4 hr), MltGEc could possess significantly higher LTG activity than AgmT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a speculation.

claim: The expression of MltGEc failed to restore gliding motility in the agmTEAEA pilA cells, even in the presence of 200 μM sodium vanillate.
source: Importantly, the expression of MltGEc failed to restore gliding motility in the agmTEAEA pilA cells, even in the presence of 200 μM sodium vanillate (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: This result suggests that AgmTEAEA still binds to PG and that in the absence of its LTG activity, AgmT does not anchor bFACs to PG.
source: Consistent with the mecillinam resistance assay (Figure 3C), this result suggests that AgmTEAEA still binds to PG and that in the absence of its LTG activity, AgmT does not anchor bFACs to PG.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on inference from the data.

claim: As MltGEc substitutes AgmT in gliding motility, it is the LTG activity, rather than specific interactions between AgmT and bFACs, that is required for gliding.
source: As MltGEc substitutes AgmT in gliding motility, it is the LTG activity, rather than specific interactions between AgmT and bFACs, that is required for gliding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is the conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Eliminating AgmT and disabling its active site significantly reduced the amounts of AglR in the pellets that contained PG.
source: Eliminating AgmT and disabling its active site significantly reduced the amounts of AglR in the pellets (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 3–5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Regardless of the presence and activity of AgmT, comparable amounts of AglR precipitated in centrifugation pellets after lysozyme treatment, indicating that AgmT does not affect the expression or stability of AglR.
source: Regardless of the presence and activity of AgmT, comparable amounts of AglR precipitated in centrifugation pellets after lysozyme treatment, indicating that AgmT does not affect the expression or stability of AglR (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 3–5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Active AgmT facilitates the association between bFACs and PG.
source: Thus, active AgmT facilitates the association between bFACs and PG.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is the conclusion from the coprecipitation data.

claim: The heterologous expression of MltGEc enriched AglR-PAmCherry in the PG-containing pellets from the ΔagmT cells but not the agmTEAEA ones.
source: Strikingly, the heterologous expression of MltGEc enriched AglR-PAmCherry in the PG-containing pellets from the ΔagmT cells but not the agmTEAEA ones (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 3–5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: AgmT connects bFACs to PG through its LTG activity.
source: These results indicate that AgmT connects bFACs to PG through its LTG activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is the main conclusion from the coprecipitation experiments.

claim: The assembly of bFACs produces wave-like deformation on cell surface.
source: The assembly of bFACs produces wave-like deformation on cell surface (Nan et al., 2011; Tchoufag et al., 2019,) suggesting that their assembly may require a flexible PG layer (Nan and Zusman, 2016; Nan et al., 2011; Nan et al., 2013; Nan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: bFAC assembly may require a flexible PG layer.
source: The assembly of bFACs produces wave-like deformation on cell surface (Nan et al., 2011; Tchoufag et al., 2019,) suggesting that their assembly may require a flexible PG layer (Nan and Zusman, 2016; Nan et al., 2011; Nan et al., 2013; Nan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: PG flexibility affects the overall stiffness of cells.
source: As a major contributor to cell stiffness, PG flexibility affects the overall stiffness of cells (Auer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The GRABS scores of the ΔagmT pilA−, and ΔagmT Pvan-MltGEc pilA− (with 200 μM sodium vanillate) cells were −0.06 ± 0.04 and −0.10 ± 0.07 (n = 4), respectively, indicating that neither AgmT nor MltGEc affects cell stiffness significantly.
source: The GRABS scores of the ΔagmT pilA−, and ΔagmT Pvan-MltGEc pilA− (with 200 μM sodium vanillate) cells were −0.06 ± 0.04 and −0.10 ± 0.07 (n = 4), respectively, indicating that neither AgmT nor MltGEc affects cell stiffness significantly.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by GRABS assay data.

claim: AgmT and MltGEc do not regulate bFAC assembly by modulating PG stiffness.
source: Whereas PG flexibility could still be essential for gliding, AgmT and MltGEc do not regulate bFAC assembly by modulating PG stiffness.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the GRABS assay data.

claim: These LTGs could connect bFACs to PG by generating structural features that are irrelevant to PG stiffness.
source: Instead, these LTGs could connect bFACs to PG by generating structural features that are irrelevant to PG stiffness.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a speculation based on the data.

claim: Compared to the trans-envelope secretion system that drives gliding in Flavobacterium johnsoniae and Capnocytophaga gingivalis, the gliding machinery of M. xanthus appears to lack a stable structure that transverses the cell envelope, especially across the PG layer.
source: Compared to the trans-envelope secretion system that drives gliding in Flavobacterium johnsoniae and Capnocytophaga gingivalis, the gliding machinery of M. xanthus appears to lack a stable structure that transverses the cell envelope, especially across the PG layer (Nan and Zusman, 2016; Hennell James et al., 2021; Shrivastava et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: In order to generate mechanical force from the fluid M. xanthus gliding machinery, the inner complex must establish solid contact with PG and push the outer complex to slide.
source: In order to generate mechanical force from the fluid M. xanthus gliding machinery, the inner complex must establish solid contact with PG and push the outer complex to slide (Faure et al., 2016; Chen and Nan, 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: AgmT is the long-sought factor that facilitates persistent gliding by connecting bFACs to PG.
source: In this work, we discovered AgmT as the long-sought factor that facilitates persistent gliding by connecting bFACs to PG.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: It is surprising that AgmT itself does not assemble into bFACs and that MltGEc substitutes AgmT in gliding.
source: It is surprising that AgmT itself does not assemble into bFACs and that MltGEc substitutes AgmT in gliding.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Rather than interacting with bFAC components directly and specifically, AgmT facilitates proper bFAC assembly indirectly through its LTG activity.
source: Thus, rather than interacting with bFAC components directly and specifically, AgmT facilitates proper bFAC assembly indirectly through its LTG activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is based on the experimental data.

claim: LTGs usually break glycan strands and produce unique anhydro caps on their ends.
source: LTGs usually break glycan strands and produce unique anhydro caps on their ends (Williams et al., 2018; Dik et al., 2017; Höltje et al., 1975; van Heijenoort, 2011; Weaver et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Because AgmT is the only LTGs that is required for gliding, it is not likely to facilitate bFAC assembly by generating such modification on glycan strands.
source: However, because AgmT is the only LTGs that is required for gliding, it is not likely to facilitate bFAC assembly by generating such modification on glycan strands.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is based on inference.

claim: E. coli MltG is a glycan terminase that controls the length of newly synthesized PG glycans.
source: E. coli MltG is a glycan terminase that controls the length of newly synthesized PG glycans (Yunck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: AgmT could generate short glycan strands and thus uniquely modify the overall structure of M. xanthus PG, such as producing small pores that retard and retain the inner subcomplexes of bFACs.
source: Likewise, AgmT could generate short glycan strands and thus uniquely modify the overall structure of M. xanthus PG, such as producing small pores that retard and retain the inner subcomplexes of bFACs (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: The M. xanthus mutants that lack active AgmT could produce PG with increased strand length, which blocks bFACs from binding to the cell wall and precludes stable bFAC assembly.
source: On the contrary, the M. xanthus mutants that lack active AgmT could produce PG with increased strand length, which blocks bFACs from binding to the cell wall and precludes stable bFAC assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is a speculation.

claim: M. xanthus MreB assembles into bFACs and positions the latter near evenly along the cell body.
source: M. xanthus MreB assembles into bFACs and positions the latter near evenly along the cell body (Nan et al., 2011; Nan et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2018; Mauriello et al., 2010; Treuner-Lange et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: MreB filaments change their orientation in accordance with local membrane curvatures and could hence respond to mechanical cues.
source: MreB filaments change their orientation in accordance with local membrane curvatures and could hence respond to mechanical cues (Hussain et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2019; Ursell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: M. xanthus does assemble bFACs in response to substrate hardness.
source: Strikingly, M. xanthus does assemble bFACs in response to substrate hardness (Figure 4C) and the assembled bFACs could distort the cell envelope, generating undulations on the cell surface (Nan et al., 2011; Nan et al., 2010; Nan et al., 2013; Tchoufag et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 4C and citations.

claim: The assembled bFACs could distort the cell envelope, generating undulations on the cell surface.
source: Strikingly, M. xanthus does assemble bFACs in response to substrate hardness (Figure 4C) and the assembled bFACs could distort the cell envelope, generating undulations on the cell surface (Nan et al., 2011; Nan et al., 2010; Nan et al., 2013; Tchoufag et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Whereas AgmT potentially modifies the entire PG layer, it is still the quasiperiodic MreB filaments that determine the loci for bFAC assembly in response to the mechanical cues from the gliding substrate.
source: Taken together, whereas AgmT potentially modifies the entire PG layer, it is still the quasiperiodic MreB filaments that determine the loci for bFAC assembly in response to the mechanical cues from the gliding substrate (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Most bacteria encode multiple LTGs that function in PG growth, remodeling, and recycling.
source: Most bacteria encode multiple LTGs that function in PG growth, remodeling, and recycling (Dik et al., 2017; Weaver et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: This work provides an example that macro bacterial machineries domesticate non-specialized LTGs for specialized functions.
source: This work provides an example that macro bacterial machineries domesticate non-specialized LTGs for specialized functions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Other examples include MltD in the Helicobacter pylori flagellum and MltE in the E. coli type VI secretion system.
source: Other examples include MltD in the Helicobacter pylori flagellum and MltE in the E. coli type VI secretion system (Roure et al., 2012; Santin and Cascales, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Based on their catalytic folds and domain arrangements, LTGs can be categorized into six distinct families.
source: Based on their catalytic folds and domain arrangements, LTGs can be categorized into six distinct families (Dik et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Both M. xanthus AgmT and E. coli MltG belong to the YceG/MltG family, which is the first identified LTG family that is conserved in both Gram-negative and -positive bacteria.
source: Both M. xanthus AgmT and E. coli MltG belong to the YceG/MltG family, which is the first identified LTG family that is conserved in both Gram-negative and -positive bacteria (Yunck et al., 2016; Dik et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: About 70% of bacterial genomes, including firmicutes, proteobacteria, and actinobacteria, encode YceG/MltG domains.
source: About 70% of bacterial genomes, including firmicutes, proteobacteria, and actinobacteria, encode YceG/MltG domains (Yunck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: The unique inner membrane localization of the YceG/MltG family and the fact that AgmT is the only M. xanthus LTG that belongs to this family could partially explain why it is the only LTG that contributes to gliding motility.
source: The unique inner membrane localization of this family and the fact that AgmT is the only M. xanthus LTG that belongs to this family (Key resources table) could partially explain why it is the only LTG that contributes to gliding motility.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is based on inference.
